title: The hunter who swept the ants
hook: a cruel hunter meets Narada, and climbs
carry: prema grows rung by rung, starting with company
tomorrow: a teacher asks a boy, who are you? his answer turns down every label.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Narada as a servant boy, and the practices Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu circles. A slight touch can begin it. Today, where it leads, with Narada again, meeting a hunter.

Chaitanya tells this story to Sanatana, Rupa's brother, in the Chaitanya Charitamrita. Narada, walking through a forest, finds deer and boars lying half-killed, left to suffer. The hunter, Mrigari, does it on purpose; his father taught him. Narada tells him plainly: the pain you give will come back to you. The hunter is shaken, and asks what to do. Break your bow, says Narada. But how will I eat? I'll see that you're fed. So the hunter breaks his bow, builds a hut by the river, and sits chanting the name beside a tulasi plant, and the villagers start bringing him food. Later, Narada comes to visit. The hunter hurries out to greet him, and stops. There are ants on the path. He bends and brushes them gently aside with his cloth before he'll take a step.
screen: `ANIMALS LEFT HALF-KILLED.` → `BREAK YOUR BOW.` → `HE SWEEPS THE ANTS ASIDE.`

segments.voice: Rupa set down a ladder, and many teachers walk this hunter up it. In paraphrase, the rungs are: faith. The company of devotees. The work of devotion. The falling away of what doesn't belong. Steadiness. Taste. Attachment. Bhava. And then prema rises. Watch the hunter go up. Faith, the moment Narada's words land. Company, Narada himself. The work: the name, by the river. Then the falling away, and nobody forces it. The cruelty simply goes, until even an ant matters. Steadiness, taste, attachment: the name he began chanting because he was told to becomes the thing he wants. Rupa describes bhava, near the top, as like a ray of the sun of prema. A ray is already sunlight; it just isn't the whole sun yet. Then prema: bhava grown dense, the heart made completely soft, with a deep sense that Krishna is one's own. That's the teaching. In this lineage, love for God isn't a switch. It grows rung by rung, and the rung after faith is people. Here the first division of Rupa's ocean ends. Tomorrow the track turns to a different Hindu path, the path of knowing, with a different teacher.
screen: `FAITH, THEN COMPANY.` · `THE CRUELTY FALLS AWAY.` · `STEADINESS, TASTE, ATTACHMENT.` · then, large: `PREMA: THE HEART MADE SOFT.`

segments.voice: Think of one practice you'd like to keep coming back to: lighting the lamp, a bhajan, a few rounds of the name, a few quiet minutes. Name what usually gets in the way: the phone, the tiredness, the late night. Then make one small plan for that moment, if this happens, then I'll do that. If you pray, offer the plan to Krishna. No rung is a grade; just notice honestly where you stand.
Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu: a book whose opening division climbs from a little faith, through company and practice, to prema, the heart made soft.
screen: `RUPA GOSWAMI'S BHAKTI RASAMRITA SINDHU — today's word`.

segments.voice: The line to keep: prema grows rung by rung, and the rung after faith is company. A hunter climbed it. Rupa's opening, complete.

howItsDone: Some Gaudiya Vaishnava communities teach this ladder to newcomers and use it to describe a devotional life that starts with faith and good company. The story of the hunter is a favorite in their classes.

fork.setup: after Narada's company and months of chanting by the river, the hunter brushes ants off his path. on Rupa's ladder, what is that?
options: the falling away of what doesn't belong: the cruelty simply went.
prema, the top rung, reached all at once.
nothing that counts; it's only good manners.
fork.reveal: After faith, company and the work of devotion, what doesn't belong falls away. Nobody forced it; the heart was softening. Bhava and prema come further up.

original.note: Sanskrit prema, the fullest love; for Rupa, bhava grown dense, the heart made completely soft.

chat.meaning: In the middle of Rupa's ladder, steadiness becomes taste, then attachment: the same practice that took effort starts to pull, the way the hunter's chanting became what he wanted.

tie.story: After Narada's company and months of chanting, Mrigari, who once left animals half-dead, stopped to brush ants off his path.

prema.meaning: the fullest love for Krishna, the heart made soft

bhava.meaning: deep love, like a ray of prema's sun

Rupa.meaning: Rupa Goswami, Chaitanya's follower who wrote this book

Krishna.meaning: worshiped in this lineage as God himself

Mrigari.meaning: the hunter in Narada's story; the name means enemy of animals

Sanatana.meaning: Sanatana Goswami, Rupa's elder brother and Chaitanya's student

tulasi.meaning: the holy basil plant, dear to Krishna

sources.ref: Chaitanya Charitamrita, Madhya-lila 24 (Chaitanya tells Sanatana of Narada and the hunter Mrigari: the half-killed animals, the broken bow, chanting by the river, and the ants brushed from the path)
Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu 1.4.15–16 (the ladder: faith, company of the good, devotional work, removal of what is unwanted, steadiness, taste, attachment, bhava, prema)
Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu 1.3.1 (bhava like a ray of the sun of prema)
Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu 1.4.1 (prema: bhava made dense, the heart thoroughly softened, marked by intense sense of mine-ness)
